newsitem.title: FRANCE: France bails out Credit Lyonnais, seeks buyers.
newsitem.headline: France bails out Credit Lyonnais, seeks buyers.

text.p: The French government said on Wednesday it would mount a third rescue of state-controlled Credit Lyonnais and declared it was open to offers to privatise the ailing bank.

"As of now, the government is ready to consider any proposals from investors for a minority or a majority stake," said the finance ministry, which originally planned to sell the bank by the year 2000.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told a news conference the new salvage operation would get the bank in shape to be privatised as the two previous rescues -- in 1994 and 1995 -- had failed to ensure its recovery.
"We're embarking on a new era," he told reporters.

The latest rescue plan would be on top of 3.9 billion francs ($764.5 million) in emergency French aid appproved on Wednesday by the European Commission, under which the government will assume costs imposed on the bank as part of last year's bailout.

The approval of the emergency package came just over a year after the European Commision cleared a 45 billion franc state bailout of the bank, whose near collapse marked the biggest scandal in recent French banking history.
The accelerated timetable for the bank's privatisation was seen as a quid pro quo for winning the European Commission's approval for the fresh state aid.

Arthuis said the sale of the bank, whose troubles stem from an expansion binge that briefly turned it into the world's biggest bank outside Japan, would take place "as quickly as possible" but was unlikely before the year end.
He said the government would be open to buyers from outside France for the bank, nationalised by President Charles de Gaulle following World War Two.
Arthuis said the third rescue plan in the pipeline would be aimed at "ensuring its (the bank's) future and making it fully competitive."

He said the government would decide whether it needed to recapitalise Credit Lyonnais after the bank reported its first half results on October 3. Some press reports have said that could cost 10 billion francs or more.
Arthuis said the emergency help for the bank, which lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994, would come from other privatisation revenues.

The aid will cover the financing shortfall for a 123 billion franc loan the bank was forced to extend at below market rates to a state-backed rescue vehicle which took over 130 billion francs of its troubled assets last year.
The European Commission had insisted that the loan be made at below market rates in order to make Credit Lyonnais share in the cost of a reckless past.

But the bank had warned that the shortfall would plunge it back into the red. The emergency help is expected to allow the bank to post a modest profit when it announces its half-year results. It eked out a 13 million franc profit in 1995.
Credit Lyonnais's rivals had complained last year's bailout was too generous but it turned out in the end to be too tough for the bank, given France's depressed banking climate.

Arthuis said the final bill to taxpayers from the Credit Lyonnais saga would only be known when the state rescue vehicle known as the Public Body for Financing and Restructuring or EPFR completes the sale of Credit Lyonnais assets. EPFR must dispose of 80 percent of the assets over a five year period.
Press reports say the final cost to taxpayers from Credit Lyonnais's expansion could eventually exceed 100 billion francs.

Arthuis said the government was intent on pinning the blame on those responsible for the bank's massive losses but French media reports suggest the government's wrath is actually aimed at preparing taxpayers to fork out more money for the bank. ($1=5.101 French Franc)
